Transcript body:
00:00:05 Maya (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros?
00:00:12 Priya: yeah hi im priya i run search at Search Fusion, we're redoing our retrieval stack, looking at a rerank flow, hi jorge liz aaron all on.
00:00:24 Jorge: hey
00:00:26 Liz: morning
00:00:28 Aaron: hi all
00:00:30 Maya: cool. Evan from infra will help on sizing. Evan quick 1-liner on Redwood options?
00:00:40 Evan (SE): sure. we have hosted api for fast start, dedicated reserved gpu pools if you need predictable throughput, and private/vpc where control plane sits in redwood but data plane can be in your vpc or on-prem. common pattern: index embeddings in a vector DB and call redwood for embeddings + optional rerank on the top k.
00:01:05 Priya: straight away we need to know latency tradeoffs. our users expect snappy suggestions under 200ms P95 for suggestions, for deep rerank we can accept up to 500ms but prefer lower. how realistic is that with a vdb fanout of 100?
00:01:22 Evan: good question. depends on embedding dim and whether rerank runs in the critical path. if you do vector fanout 100 with 1536-dim vectors and then call a 7B reranker, tail latency can creep up. typical solution: do topK 100 coarse retrieval, then run a lightweight re-ranker on the host or use redwood caching for cached prefixes. with dedicated you can pin GPUs and guarantee throughput so P95s are much tighter.
00:01:56 Priya: when you say "pin" do you mean one GPU per model replica? we're concerned about concurrent queries spikes during peak.
:01:59 Jorge (overlap): and cost — we dont want to massively overprovision.
00:02:05 Evan: yeah overlap — with dedicated you reserve capacity, you can configure pool size and autoscale policy with burst capacity. you can also choose quantized model variants for lower memory footprints to fit more replicas per GPU.
00:02:18 Liz: what's the viability of 512-dim embeddings? we've been using 1536 dims from our current vendor but curious whether lower dims + rerank gives similar relevance and big cost wins.
00:02:31 Evan: 512 can be fine for many passagish retrieval tasks, especially if you do hybrid rerank. the trick is quality regression — you need evals on your prompts. ops wise 512 reduces vector db storage and compute in similarity search; it also reduces transfer time between services. many customers do a pilot with both dims and compare recall/precision + tail latency.
00:02:50 Priya: ok good. can Redwood run those two dims side-by-side in a pilot? we want A/B on relev and measure tail.
00:02:58 Maya: yes we can. Evan will spin up bench with configurable dims and produce per-route P95, P99 and throughput.
00:03:05 Aaron: security questions — we need SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS for keys, audit logs. if we do private deployment we need bring-your-own-kms.
00:03:16 Maya: understood. we have SOC2 reports and KMS integrations. with private you can manage keys, with dedicated there's options to integrate with your cloud KMS. we'll send the security pack.
00:03:27 Aaron: great. also audit log retention and ability to purge playback — is that supported?
00:03:33 Evan: yes configurable retention in Console, and private deployments can be configured to avoid storing request payloads if you need strict controls.
00:03:42 Priya: back to architecture — our current plan is vector DB (we use an open-source index currently) for initial recall then call rerank. we worry about the extra hop to hosted api adding 50-150ms. any mitigation?
00:03:56 Evan: options: 1) deploy reranker co-located with vector DB in your VPC via Redwood Private — minimizes network hop. 2) use Redwood Dedicated in same region with warmed KV cache and batching to reduce per-token latency. 3) hybrid: do rough rerank in-house and only call Redwood for heavy responses or TTR (top-to-rank) refresh.
00:04:18 Jorge: what's the KV cache you're mentioning?
00:04:21 Evan: it's prefix cache for autoregs? sorry bad shorthand — kv cache refers to key-value cache for transformer activations when doing multi-turn, but for rerank flows we mean response caching and prefix caching so repeated requests are served zero-cost. also embedding cache for identical documents.
00:04:37 Priya: there was some vendor that recommended sharded fanout vs single big fanout — any opinion?
00:04:42 Evan: sharded fanout at the vector db side helps parallelize similarity search; Redwood's routing can also fanout across model variants or regions. for high qps, sharding your vectors across nodes is standard. for rerank, you want to limit per-request topK to keep latency predictable.
00:04:58 Liz: on the cost side, can you sketch the cost difference hosted vs dedicated for a 100 qps steady workload?
00:05:05 Maya: short answer: hosted is easiest and usually cheaper for low QPS; dedicated becomes economical as sustained QPS grows because you get reserved capacity and lower per-token pricing. we'll send a rough sketch for that 100 qps case.
00:05:17 Priya: what about cold-start latencies with hosted? we saw some vendors had warmup issues causing spikes.
00:05:24 Evan: warm-start is real. hosted has warm pools; dedicated with pinned replicas will have lower cold tail. we can also pre-warm with synthetic traffic during pilot.
00:05:32 Speaker 6: are there limits on concurrent streams?
00:05:35 Evan: streaming's supported but for rerank it's usually unary. concurrent streams limited by pool size — we'll provide exact concurrency numbers in the bench results.
00:05:45 Priya: we also use strict data residency in EU for some customers. can you deploy private in eu and integrate with our kms?
00:05:52 Maya: yes private and dedicated both support region pinning and KMS integrations; if you need on-prem we also have partner options for air-gapped setups.
00:06:01 Jorge: on the engineering side, what telemetry do we get? traces, token-level costs, per-route latencies?
00:06:07 Evan: Console exposes per-route and per-model dashboards, token cost breakdowns, traces, and ingestion-level metrics. we'll expose a tracing hook so you can connect to your existing observability.
00:06:18 Priya: hypotheticals: we run a peak of 400 qps for 30 minutes. do you recommend autoscale or dedicated overprovisioning?
00:06:26 Evan: for that burst profile you can use dedicated with burst capacity or hosted with autoscale; dedicated provides better SLO guarantees if it's a business-critical spike. hosted can handle bursts but pricing may spike.
00:06:37 Liz: do you support custom model fine-tuning for the reranker or is it zero-shot?
00:06:43 Evan: we support bringing your own tuned models and we also provide instruction-tuning paths. for small rerank models, fine-tuning is common. we also support quantized variants to reduce memory.
00:06:53 Priya: about vector DB integration — we use an open-source db with gRPC. is there an adapter model?
00:06:59 Evan: we integrate with common vector DBs via standard APIs; for custom setups we provide SDKs and a lightweight adapter pattern. part of benching is to validate network perf to your index.
00:07:10 Priya: ok can we walk through a proposed pilot?
00:07:13 Maya: suggested pilot: 2 weeks, produce A/B with 512 vs 1536 dims, measure recall/lift, P95/P99, throughput at 100 and 400 qps, and run a 24-hour smoke at target qps. we'll sign up you to a sandbox project with limited data.
00:07:28 Priya: good. timelines?
00:07:30 Maya: kickoff after we share security packs and you accept NDA. propose kickoff 12/14.
00:07:35 Aaron: quick legal Q — we need PCI/PHI handling notes? not in scope for public search but for some datasets might be relevant.
00:07:43 Maya: we have compliance add-ons, we can map controls. Evan will include relevant notes.
00:07:48 Jorge: bench specifics: can Evan simulate our query shape? many of our queries are short head queries and long tail queries that hit docs of 1-2k tokens.
00:07:58 Evan: yes, please send a sample workload. we'll run a tail-latency focused bench, include simulated doc sizes, and test both brute-force and HNSW-ish indexes in fanout.
00:08:12 Liz: for reranker model size, are 7B models reasonable? or should we look at 2.7B?
00:08:18 Evan: 7B gives better quality but costs more and increases latency; 2.7B or even tiny 1.3B cross-encoders can be surprisingly effective if you pair with good candidate recall. this is why A/B needed.
00:08:29 Priya: also curious about embeddings upsert throughput — we need to reindex daily 40k docs, sometimes burst to 150k. can Redwood handle that?
00:08:38 Evan: embed upsert throughput depends on pool size; dedicated with concurrent runners handles this fine. you can batch upserts to reduce per-item overhead. we'll include a sample sizing for daily 150k doc reindex.
00:08:51 Maya: ok we're closing on time. recap: Redwood will send security pack, sketch pricing for both hosted and 8 GPU dedicated pool, and SE will run bench comparing 512/1536 dims and 2 reranker sizes, produce P95/P99 and throughput. customer to share sample workloads and confirm kickoff date.
00:09:08 Priya: yep, we'll send queries/tarball and confirm 12/14.
00:09:13 Jorge: thanks all
00:09:15 Evan: i'll follow up with a bench plan and schedule.
00:09:19 Maya: thanks everyone.
